title: Alternative inheritances: Samaritans, the scrolls and Christian authority
heading: Introduction
text: Who may claim an inheritance shared with people they regard as mistaken? That question connects Samaritan traditions, the Dead Sea Scrolls and competing Christian accounts of authority. The connections become more useful when each one names what it compares: a textual reading, a sacred place, a calendar, a teacher or a claimed succession. Similar disputes do not automatically establish a single historical lineage. This reading guide connects the existing Samaritan texts and sacred authority article, the Jesus and Dead Sea Scrolls conversation, Qumran Text History and The Teacher, Thomas and Gnostic transmission. The cross-reference matrix below identifies the relationship and its evidential limit. New editorial connections are dated separately from the preserved conversations.

title: Alternative inheritances: Samaritans, the scrolls and Christian authority
heading: A shared Torah is not a shared institutional allegiance
text: The material starting point is 4QpaleoExodᵐ, also catalogued as 4Q22, an Exodus manuscript from Qumran written in paleo-Hebrew script. Its textual agreements with the Samaritan Pentateuch include expansions that bring parallel passages into closer agreement. Scholarship often groups such witnesses under the label pre-Samaritan. That label describes a textual relationship; it does not identify the copyist's ethnicity, the manuscript's owner or the sanctuary its readers recognized. [1][2] The useful bridge is therefore specific: the Samaritan Pentateuch preserves features with counterparts among ancient Judaean Desert manuscripts. Its entire text cannot be dismissed as a late invention simply because it differs from the later standard Jewish text. Nor does the existence of 4Q22 prove that a complete, independent Samaritan library enjoyed uniform authority across the region. A manuscript attests a textual witness; claims about a community's canon and the social reach of that witness need additional evidence. The manuscripts and movements study supplies the next question: what survives, where, and through whom? The Dead Sea Scrolls and Jewish diversity chapter distinguishes textual variation from the authority of whole books. That distinction prevents a discovery about wording from silently becoming a conclusion about a canon.

title: Alternative inheritances: Samaritans, the scrolls and Christian authority
heading: Gerizim readings need passage-by-passage comparison
text: Deuteronomy 12:5 offers a concrete entry point. The Samaritan form describes the place God has chosen; the Masoretic form speaks of the place God will choose. Posen Library provides Benyamim Tsedaka's translation alongside an explanation of the contrast. The Samaritan reading is understood within a tradition centered on Mount Gerizim. That is a textual and interpretive comparison, not an archaeological demonstration that either community's entire account of the past is correct. [3] Deuteronomy 27:4 and the Gerizim composition attached to the Decalogue are further, distinct problems. Do not treat all passages mentioning Gerizim as a single editorial event. Nor should the older claim that 4QpaleoExodᵐ simply lacked the Gerizim composition be repeated as an uncontested observation. In 2022 Hila Dayfani argued, using material and textual reconstruction of the relevant columns, that the composition belonged to this scroll. Her article challenges a familiar division between a pre-Samaritan base and a later Gerizim addition. [4] The distinction between preserved wording and reconstructed missing text matters. Dayfani's reconstruction is a scholarly argument about the manuscript, not a newly intact fragment displaying every disputed line. This guide consulted the university-hosted abstract rather than independently redoing the reconstruction. It therefore reports the proposal and its implications without declaring the debate closed. Even a successful reconstruction would not, on its own, identify the manuscript's readers as members of a Samaritan institution. This is the precise research bridge from sacred authority back to Qumran textual history: list the witness, passage, reading and uncertainty before assigning it to a community. Script, textual affiliation, ownership and religious identity are related questions, not interchangeable labels.

title: Alternative inheritances: Samaritans, the scrolls and Christian authority
heading: Sacred place and the community's own account
text: Samaritans are a living Israelite tradition, not merely a Christian illustration or an ancient deviation defined by an opponent. The Israelite Samaritan Information Institute presents its community as preserving Israel's inheritance, with Gerizim central to its sacred history and the five books of Moses central to its canon. Its own account locates a foundational priestly breach in the story of Eli and Shiloh, well before the Babylonian exile. That self-presentation should be identified as the community's tradition, rather than replaced by the claim that Samaritan identity begins as a reaction to Jerusalem. [5] Material history and inherited sacred history need separate treatment. The archaeological sanctuary on Gerizim belongs to a historical inquiry about buildings, inscriptions and phases of use. The Palestinian submission on UNESCO's Tentative List describes the site and distinguishes surviving remains from Samaritan belief. It is a state-submitted heritage description, not UNESCO certification of every historical or theological claim. [6] Read the Samaritan and Jewish Texts conversation alongside the developed article, then move to Sacred inheritance and rival continuations. The organizing question is what each claimant retains and contests. A community's self-definition deserves accurate presentation even when a historical claim remains disputed.

title: Alternative inheritances: Samaritans, the scrolls and Christian authority
heading: Qumran disputes do not mean rejection of every Temple
text: The Library of Congress's account of 4QMMT, or Some Works of the Torah, describes legal disagreements concentrated on the Temple and its ritual, with separation explained in relation to those disagreements. Its 4Q321 calendrical witness illustrates another dimension of communal order: the scheduling of priestly service and festivals. These are concrete reasons to connect the scrolls to a wider inquiry about authority. They do not show that every scroll represents one party or that the collection rejected the idea of a legitimate Temple altogether. [7] A competing sacred site and a dispute over the conduct of a sanctuary are different kinds of disagreement. The comparison with Gerizim is strongest when it asks who determines proper worship, not when it makes all parties members of an identical anti-Jerusalem movement. Likewise, the familiar identification of the Qumran community with the Essenes is a historical reconstruction, not the name written on every manuscript. [7] The Jesus and Dead Sea Scrolls conversation belongs beside this comparison, but its archived AI reply remains evidence of what was discussed, not a substitute for current source verification. Messianic language, purification and covenant claims are starting points for comparison. A proposed transfer between communities needs a plausible date, carrier and distinctive textual or social evidence. For the separate question of manuscript dates and the Teacher, read the Dead Sea Scrolls evidence review. It distinguishes radiocarbon measurements and handwriting-model estimates from a proposed identification of an ancient person. Textual affinity with the Samaritan Pentateuch does not resolve that dating or identity question.

title: Alternative inheritances: Samaritans, the scrolls and Christian authority
heading: John 4 supplies a direct Christian comparison
text: There is no need to reach Christianity only through a hypothetical chain of intermediaries. John 4:19–24 explicitly stages a dispute about worship on the Samaritan mountain and in Jerusalem. The Gospel's Jesus anticipates worship in spirit and truth while retaining the passage's asymmetrical claim that salvation is from the Jews. The text should not be reduced either to a simple endorsement of Samaritan claims or to a generic rejection of all inherited identity. [8] This is direct evidence that a Christian literary work engages Samaritan sacred geography. It is not proof that its author belonged to Qumran, that the scene is an unmediated transcript, or that later Christian groups descended institutionally from Samaritan priests. It gives Thomas, John and the Synoptics a specific lateral connection: compare how authority is relocated, who speaks and what remains contested.

title: Alternative inheritances: Samaritans, the scrolls and Christian authority
heading: Competing apostolic claims: name the source and claimant
text: For Christian succession, Clement of Alexandria, Stromata VII.17, is more useful than an undifferentiated category of secret Gnostic lineages. Clement reports claims connecting Basilides with Glaucias, described as Peter's interpreter, and Valentinus with Theudas, linked to Paul. He presents those claims while arguing for his own account of the church's priority. This is evidence that rival apostolic pedigrees were asserted and contested. It is not independent verification that each pedigree is historically accurate. [9] The Coptic Apocalypse of Peter provides a different kind of evidence: a revelation framed around Peter that attacks some people claiming the titles of bishop and deacon. Its literary allocation of privileged knowledge challenges rival Christian authority from within a Christian account of revelation. It does not preserve a chain of Samaritan-to-Qumran succession. [10] Read the laughing Jesus study for the text's distinctive crucifixion scene and its limits as political evidence. These examples sharpen the Teacher-to-Gnostic transmission inquiry. The recurring problem is control of an inheritance; the mechanisms differ. A shared Torah, an alternative sanctuary, an interpretation of prophetic scripture, a reported teacher-list and an apostolic revelation must be compared on their own terms. Calling them the exact same tradition would replace the historical question with its desired answer.

title: Alternative inheritances: Samaritans, the scrolls and Christian authority
heading: Cross-reference matrix: alternative inheritances
text: Follow the matrix by question rather than assuming a chronological chain. Textual affinity identifies shared readings or scribal practices. Comparative structure identifies a similar authority problem. Direct literary engagement means a work actually discusses the other tradition. Reported succession means an ancient author records a pedigree claim. None of these labels by itself means demonstrated institutional descent. The same matrix appears in a compact panel on the connected reader pages. It links outward to the broader inquiry, so the Samaritan and scrolls material does not become a closed loop.

title: Alternative inheritances: Samaritans, the scrolls and Christian authority
heading: Use the navigation already present
text: The wiki already has a connection explorer, parallel timelines and a working book route. The useful organizational improvement is to give their connections explicit reasons and evidential limits, then place them where a reader encounters the relevant problem. A flat file layout does not prevent a rich argument map; unnamed relationships and disconnected reading routes do. Keep three levels visible: preserved conversation, developed interpretation and source review. A dated editorial bridge may disagree with a source conversation without rewriting what its speakers said. For chronology, distinguish an event, the composition of a work and the copying of a surviving manuscript. For authority, distinguish a community's own claim from an opponent's description and an editor's historical reconstruction.

title: Alternative inheritances: Samaritans, the scrolls and Christian authority
heading: Sources and access notes
text: 1. Emanuel Tov, Textual Harmonization in Exodus 1–24, TC: A Journal of Biblical Textual Criticism 22 (2017), especially p. 15. Publicly indexed excerpts consulted for 4QpaleoExodᵐ, 4QExod-Levᶠ and harmonization. Direct PDF retrieval timed out; no complete independent collation is claimed. 2. Robert T. Anderson and Terry Giles, The Samaritan Pentateuch: An Introduction to Its Origin, History, and Significance for Biblical Studies, SBL, 2012, pp. 46–48. Publicly indexed publisher excerpts consulted for the terminology and manuscript identity; full PDF retrieval was unavailable. See also Ingrid Hjelm's 2020 survey and university abstract, which treats both traditions in their own right. 3. The Samaritan Pentateuch, Deuteronomy 12:5, Posen Library. Visible introduction and Benyamim Tsedaka translation inspected for the chosen-place contrast. This is a passage comparison, not a full critical edition. 4. Hila Dayfani, 4QpaleoExodᵐ and the Gerizim Composition, Journal of Biblical Literature 141.4 (2022), 673–698, DOI 10.15699/jbl.1414.2022.5. University-hosted abstract inspected. Its material reconstruction is reported as the author's argument; the full article and fragment measurements were not independently reviewed here. 5. Israelite Samaritan history, Israelite Samaritan Information Institute, especially the sections on Joshua, the schism, Babylonian invasion and family lineages. Consulted as a community self-presentation, not independent confirmation of its entire chronology or population figures. 6. Mount Gerizim and the Samaritans, submitted by the Permanent Delegation of Palestine to UNESCO, 2012. Heritage-site description and disclaimer inspected. The submission's content is the submitting state's responsibility. 7. The Qumran Community, Library of Congress exhibition, especially the Calendrical Document and Torah Precepts entries. Institutional description of 4Q321 and 4QMMT; its older interpretive framework is not a comprehensive review of present scholarship. 8. John 4, especially verses 19–24, World English Bible. Primary literary comparison; not used as an unmediated account of every historical Samaritan or early Christian view. 9. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata VII.17, public-domain translation hosted by New Advent. The passage reporting Glaucias, Basilides, Theudas and Valentinus was checked. Clement's polemical evaluation is kept distinct from the claims he reports. 10. Coptic Apocalypse of Peter, translated by James Brashler and Roger A. Bullard. Revelation to Peter and criticism of bishops and deacons checked. The wiki's linked study supplies manuscript locators and additional references.
